What they're saying: "We are focused on getting unprecedented resources to the Districts that will decide the majority," Johnson said in a statement to Axios. "With this continued momentum, we are in place to defy history and defend the House to save America from the far-left!" State of play: House Republicans have a cash advantage over Democrats. The NRCC ended August with $13 million more in cash on hand than the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, its largest-ever advantage at this point in an election cycle. But the House battlefield has continued to move toward Democrats. Cook Political Report shifted 15 House races toward…

33e1d7779a:3927178bef3f8d05.title: Americans' trust in the food safety net is spoiling
33e1d7779a:3927178bef3f8d05.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:3927178bef3f8d05.summary: Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Americans' confidence in the safety of food on grocery store shelves — and in the federal government's ability to regulate it — has plummeted to new lows according to a new Gallup poll. The big picture: Simultaneous illness outbreaks put federal regulators under a microscope earlier this year, as layoffs across the nation's health apparatus were already causing food safety angst. By the numbers: Less than half of U.S. adults have a great deal (11%) or a fair amount (36%) of confidence in the federal government to ensure food safety, according to the poll, which was conducted last month. On the flip side, a majority have not much or no confidence in the government's ability to police their food — a first in Gallup's trend, which has been intermittent for two decades. Zoom out: Meanwhile, Americans' confidence in the food sold at grocery stores has mirrored that drop, falling to a record low of 65% saying they are somewhat or very confident. That share has plunged from the 81% recorded in 2019. Zoom in: That growing food safety suspicion is driven by Democrats and independents, while Republicans have actually become more confident in grocery store food. The partisan chasm over the federal government's ability to ensure food safety has flipped — and widened — under the second Trump administration. In 2024, half of Republicans had a great deal or fair amount of confidence in the government to ensure food safety, while nearly three-quarters of Democrats agreed. By 2025, Democrats' confidence fell to 48%, and to 30% in 2026. Republicans, meanwhile, found new faith, with their confidence climbing from 62% in 2025 to 70% to 2026. Catch up quick: This year's polling occurred during and after the federal government declared the end of an outbreak of Cyclospora, a parasite that caused stomach illnesses, two deaths and saw more than 500 hospitalizations across 21 states. Federal health officials eventually traced the rapidly spreading…

33e1d7779a:c941dfee3ef80b00.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
33e1d7779a:c941dfee3ef80b00.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:c941dfee3ef80b00.summary: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , U.S. officials said. Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier. The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response. "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios. A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time. "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election. Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues. An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning. Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions. "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The…

33e1d7779a:f7227b2b31e15330.title: Student protest unrest spreads across Europe
33e1d7779a:f7227b2b31e15330.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:f7227b2b31e15330.summary: Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France. Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions. Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding. There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France. In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1. The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education. In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews , including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations. In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France." Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports . In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ . In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau . In…

33e1d7779a:50b13d332a6ebc05.title: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
33e1d7779a:50b13d332a6ebc05.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:50b13d332a6ebc05.summary: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration on Wednesday over its campaign-style ads . Why it matters: The DNC alleges the ads, which have drawn considerable backlash as they were originally paid for with taxpayer money, violate a several federal laws, including one addressing propaganda. What they're saying: "These ads are a clear violation of the Congressional ban on the use of appropriated funds for "publicity or propaganda purposes," the DNC's legal counsel wrote in the lawsuit . "The President has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day 'midterm convention,' and repeatedly directed voters to 'pretend that I am on the ballot," it added. "As the 2026 midterm election has approached, Republican poll numbers have plummeted in both traditional battlegrounds and typically favorable states, and Democrats are poised to take control of Congress, governor's mansions, and state legislatures around the country." Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: The lawsuit alleges the ads were crafted by the White House to boost the president's approval ratings and assist Republican candidates. The complaint largely focuses on its allegation that the ads were paid for with money originally allocated for Customs and Border Protection that was rerouted for the TV spots. The DNC argues that the ads violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the Antideficiency Act, and the Purpose Act. Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:86a6a057d3055806.title: Trump's midterm strategists draw scrutiny over Russia-aligned work
33e1d7779a:86a6a057d3055806.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:86a6a057d3055806.summary: President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there. Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation. What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday. "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C." "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!" The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each." Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S. A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment. The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous." Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration. "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said. "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting…

33e1d7779a:08b5264d82365075.title: Syria considering sending troops to Yemen to fight Houthis
33e1d7779a:08b5264d82365075.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:08b5264d82365075.summary: Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but hasn't decided. Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said. But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam. Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week. The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis. While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request. Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said. Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria. Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed.…

33e1d7779a:af2d5c2517d55f4d.title: Exclusive: Inside Trump's AI science summit
33e1d7779a:af2d5c2517d55f4d.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:af2d5c2517d55f4d.summary: President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development. Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. The White House is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access. The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools. Leading scientists and "innovators" will attend the summit, the White House says. Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. It highlights industry's increasing role in driving research and development, plus new mechanisms for funding and organizing research. Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery. In July, the White House announced that the effort would be expanded to more than 15 federal agencies. Last week, the White House held another AI summit that focused on the rollout of America.gov, which aims to streamline government services using AI.

33e1d7779a:f0c7e7265c39a80b.title: Microsoft looks to reboot the AI PC with Nvidia
33e1d7779a:f0c7e7265c39a80b.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:f0c7e7265c39a80b.summary: Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom. Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud. Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599. "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said. Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16. On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows. The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature. Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds what their companies' AI budgets can afford, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective. "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said. And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.

33e1d7779a:e5ed4e0e6628fdde.title: Americans don't want taxpayer dollars funding campaign ads: poll
33e1d7779a:e5ed4e0e6628fdde.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:e5ed4e0e6628fdde.summary: Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll . Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition. While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent). Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters. The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members. Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president. Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads. Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning"…

33e1d7779a:ab80b50c6ce52b89.title: Why France is a warning sign for the markets
33e1d7779a:ab80b50c6ce52b89.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:ab80b50c6ce52b89.summary: The good news about the epic shifts in global bond markets is that they mostly reflect economic fundamentals, not the kinds of panicky swings seen in a crisis. The bad news is that there's a risk the disruptions metastasize into a broader crisis in an era of fractured politics across major democracies. The big picture: Turmoil in the streets this week in France is the latest sign of hazards that await elected leaders who try to address yawning fiscal deficits head-on. They are squeezed between voters who want to maintain public benefit levels and tax levels and a bond market that is resetting long-term interest rates higher — meaning that carrying on with wide deficits will come at a greater and greater cost to service debt. That's why even what has been a relatively orderly repricing so far carries risks that are bigger than just high mortgage or corporate borrowing rates. Driving the news: The relentless upward march of bond yields continued Wednesday morning. The French 10-year yield soared 0.18 percentage point, to 4.93%. French yields are also surging relative to other countries that use the euro, especially Germany — the kind of fragmentation seen in the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s that originated in Greece . But France is not alone. U.K. 10-year yields are up 0.12 point, to 5.49%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is up 0.08 point Wednesday morning, reaching 5.36%, the highest since 2002. Reality check: These are massive moves in markets that form the bedrock of global financial markets. And yet they don't appear to be driven by the kind of crisis dynamics and forced selling that fueled bond market volatility in the 2008 crisis, the 2014 Treasury flash crash and the March 2020 pandemic. Rather, they've been driven by bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and deficit-running sovereign governments, exacerbated by surging energy prices that increase inflation risk. What they're saying: "When you look at outright yield levels and/or…

33e1d7779a:9f81f38914b6209d.title: Raskin seeks to preserve Trump's D.C. "propaganda" in Smithsonian
33e1d7779a:9f81f38914b6209d.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:9f81f38914b6209d.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) introduced legislation Wednesday that would direct the Smithsonian to preserve and display artifacts he said reflect the rise of "governmental propaganda" under President Trump . Why it matters: The bill will almost certainly fail in a Republican-controlled Congress. But it could preview how Democrats would scrutinize the president's use of taxpayer dollars to promote his image if they regain control in November. Trump's drive to remake D.C.'s physical and cultural landscape in his image can be seen in banners bearing his face on government buildings and attempts to rebrand institutions with his name . The administration also unveiled a plan last month to post warnings accusing Smithsonian leaders of pushing "personal, radical ideologies." Driving the news: Raskin's bill directs the secretary of the Smithsonian to collect and display Trump's sprawling portraits hung outside of federal agencies at the Museum of American History. It also calls for preserving signage or "artifacts" related to Trump's planned warning signs accusing the museum of "Ideological Capture." The proposed new exhibit would also include narratives from Americans "who resisted and opposed the rise in authoritarianism." It also calls for signage stating, in part, "Donald Trump ordered the installation of these signs without any Congressional authorization as required by the Constitution." What they're saying: " Unlike President Trump's project of censoring, whitewashing and fictionalizing American history, my legislation will forever preserve his manifestations of authoritarian narcissism and his propagandistic assault on American history and American democracy," Raskin said in a statement. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: The Smithsonian has been caught in the crosshairs of the president's D.C. residency and his government-wide DEI purge that has targeted so-called "woke ideology." Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie…

33e1d7779a:0ed177868d2cd8b7.title: "The beginning of a new scientific paradigm": Zuckerberg's Biohub, U.S. and Google build virtual cell
33e1d7779a:0ed177868d2cd8b7.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:0ed177868d2cd8b7.summary: Mark Zuckerberg's Biohub is partnering with Google and the federal government in its ambitious effort to use AI for generating vast quantities of biological data that can predict how cells behave. Why it matters: The ultimate goal is an AI model that lets scientists test potential experiments virtually, helping them identify the most promising ones before spending the time and money to perform them in the lab. AI is capable of understanding proteins and other pieces of biology, but modeling an entire living cell is orders of magnitude more complex — and researchers don't yet have enough of the right data to do it. Driving the news: Biohub, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, Meta and a collection of scientific organizations are collaborating to create and standardize data for what Biohub calls a "universal virtual cell." The big picture: The goal is to use AI to explore many more scientific questions in biology virtually, allowing scientists to reserve expensive lab work for experiments most likely to teach them something important. "If we can put more and more reasoning and intelligence into every single question that we actually ask in the lab, the value of those empirical results will be far greater," Biohub head of science Alex Rives told Axios. Much of AI's recent progress has come from combining better algorithms, more computing power and enormous amounts of data. Biology presents an additional challenge: Much of the information AI needs doesn't exist yet and has to be painstakingly measured from the physical world. "We're at the beginning of a new scientific paradigm with AI," Rives said. Yes, but: Biology is harder than many other AI domains because researchers need what Rives calls "empirical AI" — models that learn from biological evidence and can accurately predict what happens in the physical world. "The big challenge in biology is to bridge that gap between compute and the digital world and…

33e1d7779a:6f2dd5ea233944e3.title: America's changing disaster risk hits energy
33e1d7779a:6f2dd5ea233944e3.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:6f2dd5ea233944e3.summary: Hurricanes have long dominated efforts to make the power system more resilient to extreme weather . But America's energy buildout is running into growing risks from severe thunderstorms. Why it matters: New energy infrastructure and data centers are being built in harm's way as severe weather risks shift , leaving more for developers and insurers to lose when storms hit. Driving the news: Severe thunderstorms account for 40% of modeled global insured catastrophe risk, compared with 27% for hurricanes , according to analysis from risk analytics firm Verisk. The U.S. accounts for $117 billion, or 68%, of Verisk's modeled global insured catastrophe losses . Threat level: A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, potentially creating more favorable conditions for powerful thunderstorms. But the effects of climate change on severe storms are complicated. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research scientist Harold Brooks told Axios that other atmospheric conditions needed for severe storms may become less favorable as the planet warms. Reality check: Verisk's Jay Guin said growing exposure, more than climate change, is the dominant driver of rising insured losses, as more and increasingly valuable property is built in harm's way. Guin says climate change contributes, but expanding development and higher reconstruction costs are much larger drivers. Zoom in: America's changing energy system is creating new kinds of exposure. Verisk is assessing risks to renewable projects in tornado- and hail-prone areas, where Guin said large hail can cause major damage to solar farms. "While they are renewable, you have a new asset class that is quite vulnerable," he said. Data-center developers must balance natural-hazard exposure against access to land, power and water. Some sites have billions in property and hardware, raising the stakes for siting and engineering. State of play: Tornado activity has increased about 10% in the Mid-South while declining by roughly the…

33e1d7779a:1960c1d025b442b3.title: Exclusive: Paxton privately blames campaign woes on Iran war, gas prices
33e1d7779a:1960c1d025b442b3.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:1960c1d025b442b3.summary: Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign in a meeting last month, telling a group of donors and lobbyists, "I don't make the decisions," according to audio obtained by Axios. Why it matters: It's a candid admission from a close Trump ally about the challenging environment Republicans face this cycle. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, was speaking to donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, D.C. The audio was provided to Axios by a person, granted anonymity because it was a private event, who was in the meeting and is opposed to Paxton. President Trump is set to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday. Driving the news: Asked by one attendee what issues are "dragging" on his campaign, Paxton responded, "It's not tariffs. ... It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," according to an audio file obtained by Axios. "When it's over $6 per gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch," he continued, adding that the rising cost of fuel "drives up food prices and everything else." The Republican candidate said affordability is "by far our biggest problem" and "why we're having a hard time with numbers." Paxton pointed to his tax cut plan — which includes new housing and health care write-offs and an expansion of the child tax credit — as his proposed remedy on affordability. "I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people. That's the only way: I can propose legislation," he said. When an attendee posited that Paxton "can't stop the war," the candidate responded "right" and said he has "no control over gas prices." "So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don't make the decisions, and I don't ... know what's behind some of the decisions," he added. What they're saying: "This is a non-story. The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump…

33e1d7779a:e5f94e130f1b7469.title: 3 years later, Netanyahu faces reckoning over Oct. 7 in Israeli election
33e1d7779a:e5f94e130f1b7469.author: Dave Lawler
33e1d7779a:e5f94e130f1b7469.summary: Israel is marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terror attacks three weeks before an election where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal culpability for the country's worst-ever security failure will be a central issue. Why it matters: Netanyahu has never looked more politically vulnerable than in the weeks after Oct. 7, but he has defied expectations by keeping his government afloat — presiding over simultaneous wars and an atmosphere of perpetual emergency. Though the polls are tight, they leave a clear path for the ultimate political survivor to hang on yet again. But Oct. 7 still looms over the country and his candidacy. The opposition lambasts him for refusing to take responsibility or allow an independent inquiry into the Hamas attacks that killed around 1,200 people. Every other senior national security official who was in office at the time of the attacks has resigned, except Netanyahu. Netanyahu's chief opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, lost his son and two nephews during the war in Gaza. Sources close to Eisenkot say he sees his main mission as replacing the man he holds responsible for allowing the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu blames the deep state. His political and media allies — as well as his wife, Sara — have even spread conspiracy theories implying Israel was betrayed by its own security chiefs. Netanyahu himself has claimed those security chiefs deliberately kept him in the dark and suggested he could have prevented the massacre if only they'd woken him up when early warning signs came in. Driving the news: Recent reporting suggests Netanyahu had at least some warning. Haaretz reported that United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu days before the attacks that Hamas was planning a major operation. Three sources with knowledge confirmed to Axios that UAE intelligence gave a general warning to its Israeli counterparts and that MBZ spoke to Netanyahu to make sure he received it.…

33e1d7779a:20d71cd0261c3ff1.title: "Not safe for kids": advocacy group urges OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT
33e1d7779a:20d71cd0261c3ff1.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:20d71cd0261c3ff1.summary: Common Sense Media is urging OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT, saying its new teen experience poses an "Unacceptable Risk" after extensive testing found shortcomings in safeguards meant to protect younger users. Why it matters: OpenAI has made protecting younger users a central part of its effort to make ChatGPT safer, but the findings suggest some of those protections may give parents more confidence than they warrant. "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice," an OpenAI spokesperson said. Driving the news: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute said it tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds. The group found ChatGPT generally did not provide instructions facilitating suicide or self-harm, eating disorders or sexual or romantic roleplay, but said it was less reliable at recognizing when a teen needed outside help. Common Sense Media said ChatGPT missed more than one in four instances in which its testers determined a crisis referral was warranted. The group also said that on more than a dozen newly created, parent-linked accounts, testers could spend up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or disordered eating without triggering a parental alert. Common Sense also found that Study Mode could be circumvented: Teens could choose "Show me the answer" and, during parent-set Study Hours, could easily bypass the rules. OpenAI confirmed to Axios that the ability to exit Study Mode during Study Hours is intentional, not a loophole. The company said it designed Study Hours as a more flexible experience after consulting education experts and teens, rather than as a hard parental lock. What they're saying: "ChatGPT is not safe for kids to use," Common Sense Media Youth Safety Institute head Tom Siegel told Axios. Siegel said that what the company announced in August still has the potential to be…

33e1d7779a:4b56013c5197b332.title: "You suck": Emmer unloads on Senate Republicans
33e1d7779a:4b56013c5197b332.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:4b56013c5197b332.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is saying out loud what House Republicans have been grumbling about for much of the year: They're fed up with the Senate. Why it matters You won't ever hear Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) or Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) talk about their Senate counterparts like this. "There are no Democrats. There are no Republicans. They are just senators," Emmer told donors last week at a closed-door fundraiser Axios attended for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.). Emmer said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) "is doing the job that he thinks he's supposed to do. There's a certain fraternity sorority that is the U.S. Senate." The intrigue: Emmer had a blunt message for senators who repeatedly say they can't pass House GOP priorities: "Don't just keep telling me 'Don't have the votes. Don't have the votes.' You suck." Emmer said he once thought as a House member that he should stay out of the filibuster debate. Now, he thinks his colleagues should "get rid of the darn filibuster." A Senate GOP aide retorted that what would "suck" would be losing the majority and that Republicans should be targeting Democrats instead of attacking their own side. Driving the news: Emmer's comments are the most critical yet from a House GOP leader, but sum up the mood inside the conference. More than a dozen Republicans paralyzed the House floor this summer in an effort to force Senate action on the SAVE America Act, the GOP's signature election bill that's become a major source of tension between the two chambers. "We're frustrated with the Senate," Emmer told Axios in an interview after the fundraiser. "We feel like we've been doing everything we were hired to do, and a lot of it goes over to the Senate and it just sits there." House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes. The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But…

33e1d7779a:f6655eff8287bcf4.title: House GOP leaders admit redistricting fell short
33e1d7779a:f6655eff8287bcf4.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:f6655eff8287bcf4.summary: House GOP leaders are now openly acknowledging that their mid-decade redistricting push didn't work out as well as they'd hoped. Why it matters: Republicans kicked off the redistricting wars hoping new maps would give them a bigger cushion against the historical headwinds facing the president's party. That advantage is looking a lot smaller than they envisioned. Driving the news: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios that Republicans won't win all 13 seats they'd hoped to gain from new maps. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," Emmer told Axios aboard a plane Thursday between campaign stops in North Carolina and Virginia. Emmer echoed House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), who told Axios last month that Republicans were unlikely to sweep all 13. Zoom in: Emmer said he'd be "surprised" if Republicans sweep all five newly drawn seats in Texas and "shocked" if they win all four in Florida . But he said Republicans are certain to pick up newly drawn seats in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee. At a fundraiser for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) on Thursday, Emmer told donors that Republicans could also offset losses with pickups in Maine and potentially North Carolina, Ohio, New Mexico and Washington. Even assuming Republicans lose five seats because of redistricting in California and Utah, pickups elsewhere give the party a path to come out ahead, Emmer told donors. State of play: Redistricting still gave Republicans an edge, just smaller than they once thought. The Cook Political Report now projects Republicans will net around four seats from redistricting alone, down from the double-digit gains Republicans once hoped to squeeze from new maps. Democrats' maps in California and Utah — in response to a new Texas map — offset the GOP gains. Some newly drawn Republican pickup opportunities have become more competitive than expected. The bottom line: Democrats need to net just three seats to win the…

33e1d7779a:a018d348e092ad03.title: CDC: Monitoring Russian plague risk, "prepared" for any threat
33e1d7779a:a018d348e092ad03.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:a018d348e092ad03.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia and says it is prepared for any threat that emerges. Why it matters: Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous form of plague and is almost always fatal unless if left untreated. The latest: President Trump told reporters Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to discuss the suspected plague case and would speak with him "very soon." Asked what U.S. intelligence was saying about the situation, Trump said officials were in "very deep discussions" and that "we'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow." Catch up quick: Darya Shipilova , a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, died after reports that she may have been exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Russian authorities say testing has not linked her death to plague or to pathogens she handled at work. However, at least five hospitals in the area remain in quarantine and almost 200 people who had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation as a precaution. What they're saying: "We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available," the CDC said in an X post Tuesday. "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely." Context: The CDC said the plague is a dangerous bacterial disease that can be treated with antibiotics, especially when caught early. Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. The CDC says "rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals" are important for keeping people safe. State of play: The concerns have drawn attention on social media and from government…

33e1d7779a:ec48210b49c9a7df.title: A brutal winter heating bill is coming for some homes
33e1d7779a:ec48210b49c9a7df.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:ec48210b49c9a7df.summary: Americans could pay far more to heat their homes with oil this winter than last, a new analysis reviewed by Axios shows, as volatile energy markets and the Iran War deepen the affordability crisis. Why it matters: Heating bills are eating into household budgets before winter sets in, with stark divides between fuel types. By the numbers: Families that heat with oil could pay about 50% more this winter than last, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), up from its 31.3% projection in mid-September. The average cost of heating a home with oil is expected to rise by about $878, costing over $2,600 this winter. By comparison, the Energy Information Administration's Winter Fuels Outlook released Tuesday projects electricity bills will rise 4% nationally, while natural gas bills will fall 9% and propane spending will drop 3%. EIA expects a smaller increase on heating oil than NEADA, projecting a 21% increase in household expenditures. Northeastern households will feel the pain most acutely: about 82% of home heating oil is consumed in the region, where some states lack robust natural gas pipelines, according to NEADA data. Just 3% of U.S. households use oil as their primary heat source, compared to about 45% using natural gas and 43% using electricity, NEADA says. The big picture: Heating oil prices are rising as global oil markets falter because of the wars in Iran and Ukraine and as refinery activity declines. "Those trends really reflect the worst-case scenario of this war, and they are going to feel it this winter, and it's unfortunate," Mark Wolfe, executive director of the NEADA, tells Axios. What they're saying: Because of the cost, some families will cut back on food or medicine, borrow from payday lenders, or turn the heat down to unsafe levels to cover their heating bills, Wolfe says. " With low-income families, sometimes states will move money around to help them, but they'll go without, " Wolfe says. Between…

33e1d7779a:851c3fc58425954f.title: Trump's PAC won't pay taxpayers back for his ads
33e1d7779a:851c3fc58425954f.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:851c3fc58425954f.summary: President Trump's super PAC will not reimburse the government for taxpayer money spent on campaign-style ads promoting the administration. Why it matters: Taxpayers have footed a multimillion-dollar bill for the advertisements, which some critics of the president have called " government propaganda ." What they're saying: "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday evening. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," he wrote, referring to a super PAC affiliated with the president. Worth noting: Federal law generally bars federal officeholders from directing spending decisions for super PACs. Zoom in: When reached for comment, a White House spokesperson told Axios that Trump's announcement "was not referring to reimbursement." Catch up quick: The White House previously defended the ads as "public service announcements" that are "clearly not political." The White House says the ads are instead meant to be patriotic, noting that Trump isn't on the ballot this year. Nonetheless, one such ad repurposes a nearly identical ad from Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, cutting it shorter and adding "Paid for by the U.S. government." Zoom out: The ads, which have run on cable and network television, including during NFL games, have cost at least $11 million since September, according to an AdImpact analysis conducted by the AP. The spots were paid for through a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up

33e1d7779a:1d12a03530109343.title: DOJ moves to strip citizenship from 40 people
33e1d7779a:1d12a03530109343.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:1d12a03530109343.summary: President Trump's Justice Department moved to revoke citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in recent months, representing what Attorney General Todd Blanche called the "largest denaturalization effort in modern history." The big picture: The Trump administration has made denaturalization a priority, moving personnel to pursue more cases and setting a goal of 250 cases by this month. Driving the news: The DOJ filed 40 denaturalization actions in district courts spanning coast to coast between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2, according to a Monday statement . "Every single one of these individuals lied their way into U.S. citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement. Context: Denaturalization cases have a high burden of proof, and to revoke someone's citizenship, the DOJ must file a revocation action in federal district court. The general grounds for revocation, per U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, are illegal procurement of naturalized citizenship or lying to get it. "For civil revocation of naturalization, the burden of proof is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence which does not leave the issue in doubt," per USCIS. Zoom in: Individuals named in Monday's statement had been convicted of or pleaded guilty to an array of offenses, including conspiracy to commit money laundering, sexual abuse of a minor and aggravated sodomy. What we're watching: The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for specifics on how many actions had been filed since the start of the second Trump administration. In April, the New York Times reported that the DOJ had identified 384 foreign-born Americans whose citizenship the department wanted to revoke. The following month, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported that USCIS lawyers had been temporarily moved to U.S. attorneys' offices to work on denaturalization cases. Go deeper: Birthright citizenship decision gives advocates short-lived sigh of relief

33e1d7779a:ce6b0447aa8dff9f.title: AI tools flood into underground cybercrime markets
33e1d7779a:ce6b0447aa8dff9f.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:ce6b0447aa8dff9f.summary: Hackers in underground cybercriminal forums are on shopping sprees for new AI tools , according to research shared first with Axios. Why it matters: AI is making once-specialized hacking capabilities cheaper and easier to buy, potentially transforming far more criminals into dangerous hackers. By the numbers: Advertisements for AI tools on underground forums and platforms surged from fewer than 50 per month in late 2025 to more than 1,400 by February, according to a report from Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center. Sellers offered access to ChatGPT Plus accounts for as little as 10 cents and jailbreak prompts to trick models into breaking their safeguards for 32 cents, per the research. Halcyon studied nearly 4,000 posts across 77 Telegram channels, 20 dark web forums and five specialized underground markets between October and May. Threat level: Companies are already losing millions of dollars to the types of cyberattacks enabled by the tools found on these underground markets. "It really goes to show you how cheap it is to conduct these activities ... which should be scary for organizations," Cynthia Kaiser, head of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of FBI Cyber, told Axios. The big picture: Cybercriminals have completely commercialized the sale and creation of these tools, often modeling software-as-a-service subscription models and online storefronts, per the report. Some sellers are now offering AI tools they tested and promoted on traditional dark web forums through easier-to-manage storefronts hosted on Telegram. "It shouldn't have been shocking to me," Kaiser said. "But what we should take away from this is also how much cybercriminals have learned throughout the years about how to sell and package — and they applied this really quickly to the AI models." Zoom in: Hackers are selling four types of AI tools: Jailbroken and stolen AI services, including prompts that allow users to strip the safety guardrails from mainstream…

33e1d7779a:8a249355b11c2ef1.title: Paramount closes historic $110B deal for Warner Bros. Discovery to create Skydance
33e1d7779a:8a249355b11c2ef1.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:8a249355b11c2ef1.summary: Paramount Skydance on Tuesday closed its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, ending a dramatic, yearlong process that rattled Hollywood, Wall Street and Washington. Why it matters: The deal creates one of the largest entertainment behemoths in the world and makes David Ellison — a lesser-known figure outside of Hollywood — one of the most powerful people in culture and business. Zoom in: The combined entity, rebranded Skydance, will house three major movie studios (Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures and Skydance), two global streamers (Paramount+ and HBO Max) and two major news networks (CNN and CBS). It will also create a cable juggernaut, marrying Paramount's Viacom channels, such as MTV, VH1 and Comedy Central, with WBD's cable networks, including TBS, TNT, Food Network and Discovery. The combination of those assets on the back end won't all be felt by consumers, but product changes are coming. The combined company, for example, plans to merge HBO Max and Paramount + into one giant unified streamer. The big picture: The transaction forced the entertainment industry and regulators around the world to confront how much consolidation is necessary for traditional media companies to compete with Big Tech. While some countries took a closer look at the deal than others, every government that required regulatory approval for the merger ultimately blessed the transaction. Although Netflix did meaningfully engage in a bidding war for WBD, it eventually abandoned its interest when the asset became too pricey. Reality check: Merger fights don't typically enter the zeitgeist for everyday Americans, but this one played into a broader societal debate around the concentration of power among the elite and the independence of federal regulators. Ellison's father, Oracle co-founder and Trump ally Larry Ellison , agreed to backstop billions of dollars of equity financing to seal the deal. Federal regulators cleared billions of dollars in equity investments from Middle…

33e1d7779a:0f215707288f40a4.title: SF Fed president: AI demand could extend energy shock
33e1d7779a:0f215707288f40a4.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:0f215707288f40a4.summary: Some companies are preparing for an AI-fueled chip squeeze that could push up prices far beyond the data center boom alone, Mary Daly, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, tells Axios. Why it matters: The Fed can usually look through supply shocks that come and go. Daly's concern is that AI, tariffs and higher energy costs could last longer than expected or compound each other — keeping inflation elevated and requiring more tightening. State of play: Daly says AI demand could spread beyond high-end chips before supply catches up, extending the shock beyond the period the Fed would normally expect to look through. "I see it less as a one-off," she says, referring to AI-driven pressure on chip and other technology prices. Daly says the Fed typically thinks in terms of shocks fading within one to three years. "This is probably further out before we get relief." "It doesn't seem like the demand for AI is going down. If anything, it seems like it's going up." Zoom in: Daly's district includes Silicon Valley and many of the companies driving the AI boom. In conversations with business contacts, she says, she's starting to hear signs that companies are bracing for tighter chip supplies — suggesting that the AI boom is beginning to alter purchasing and product-design decisions outside the data center sector. Daly says that some firms are seeking forward contracts for memory chips "so that they know they have a supplier." Those contracts can give companies more certainty about future supply — a notable development in the memory sector , a fast-depreciating market where firms typically have less reason to lock in chips ahead of time. Daly says some companies are also beginning to "reengineer their products" to rely less on chips, giving them more room to maneuver in case supplies tighten. "I see that as a signal that there is a little bit of concern this is going to spread more broadly." What to watch: The fear is that the scramble for AI hardware begins…

ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.title: Beyond the Paycheck: Using Fringe Benefits to Attract a Broader Pool of Applicants
ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.author: Thea S. Zoellner
ecbefe1924:a58a8203f9eb453d.summary: Many firms in tight labor markets recruit for highly gender-segregated occupations, leaving them, in effect, drawing from only half the potential labor pool. We study how firms can use fringe benefits to attract workers and influence occupational choice. Unlike occupation-specific recruiting strategies, fringe benefits can be added to any occupation; they are also easily tailored, implemented, and scaled. Using a personalized and incentivized discrete choice experiment, we present participants with job options that match their skills and work task preferences. Within each option, we vary salary, occupation, and fringe benefits that adolescents had classified as gender-neutral, male-typed, or female-typed. We find that fringe benefits are highly valued: their effect is around a third as large as having prior interest in the occupation. Neutral and stereotypical benefits in particular improve perceptions of the firm across multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we find substantial gender differences. Female-typed benefits deter male participants, whereas all other benefit-participant combinations have a positive effect. Female participants value benefits more when those benefits are paired with an atypical occupation, and we find suggestive evidence that this reflects benefits alleviating concerns about limited support in such roles. In addition, male-typed benefits can increase the attractiveness of gender-atypical occupations for female participants. Female participants who consider atypical occupations place relatively higher value on these benefits and tend to exhibit less traditionally feminine preferences. We also find suggestive evidence that anticipated social reactions, particularly from parents, accompany these choices.

ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.title: How to Increase the Mental Well-Being of Your Employees? An Overview of Research Testing Interventions in the Workplace
ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.author: Baert, Stijn
ecbefe1924:b320ea52cb495871.summary: This systematic literature review provides a state-of-the-art overview of the effectiveness of workplace interventions aimed at improving workersâ€™ mental well-being. Specifically, it examines which types of interventions are effective for which aspects of mental well-being, both in the short and long term. To this end, we identify 125 randomised controlled trials comprising 147 interventions that vary in their objectives (prevention, treatment, or reintegration), targets (workers or work), methods (cognitive, meditation-based, physical, ergonomic, organisational, or multimethod) and delivery channels (offline, online or hybrid). Mental well-being outcomes are classified as biological and self-reported indicators of the three components of subjective mental well-being (evaluative, affective, and eudaimonic well-being). Overall, we find that, for preventing and treating early mental health symptoms, cognitive or meditation-based interventions targeting personal coping resources appear most promising. In contrast, successful reintegration seems to require a combination of cognitive and organisational interventions, with the latter addressing job demands and resources.

ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.title: Meetings
ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.author: Yaling Xu
ecbefe1924:131e88a7c1c49d4f.summary: Why do we have so many meetings? Few workplace features are so scorned, yet seemingly so necessary. This paper provides the first large-scale economic evidence on workplace meetings using an original survey of more than 9, 000 workers linked to matched employer–employee administrative data from Norway. We show that meetings are both common and costly, consuming an average of 12 percent of work hours and 14 percent of firm wage bills. Planning, problem solving, information sharing, and project coordination account for the majority of meeting activity. High-paying and high-revenue firms devote more resources to meetings despite facing a substantially higher opportunity cost of employee time. Meeting frequency and intensity are positively related to worker wage growth. Workers in meeting-intensive firms report greater on-the-job learning, and interactions with more senior colleagues are associated with stronger wage growth, suggesting that knowledge transmission within firms is an important mechanism. Meetings are the broccoli of work – widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.

ecbefe1924:3445fc66ea310c41.title: Signals, Steps, and Setbacks: Age Discrimination in a Laddered Labor Market
ecbefe1924:3445fc66ea310c41.author: Xiaoyu Xia
ecbefe1924:3445fc66ea310c41.summary: We study age discrimination in a labor market with a job ladder, where worker productivity is revealed over time. Using data from a large Chinese recruitment platform that links job postings, applications, and employer responses, we document sharp declines in applications and callbacks at posted age cutoffs. Discrimination operates in both directions: older applicants are disadvantaged in entry-level jobs, while younger applicants are less likely to be hired into managerial roles. A model of statistical discrimination with imperfect signal screening explains these patterns. Consistent with the model, older applicants to entry-level jobs are negatively selected relative to their peers.

ecbefe1924:92bf3f127abbc04d.title: Female-Targeted Hiring Subsidies, Firm Learning, and Women’s Employment
ecbefe1924:92bf3f127abbc04d.author: Anna Raute
ecbefe1924:92bf3f127abbc04d.summary: Women often struggle to re-enter employment after career breaks, possibly because employers are uncertain about their productivity. We study whether hiring subsidies help firms overcome this uncertainty and hire from this group. Exploiting an Italian policy that temporarily cut payroll taxes for women hired from non-employment, we find that firms persistently hire more women with career breaks, including mothers, following subsidy adoption. Consistent with employer learning about target-group productivity, firms with better initial matches later hire more from this group. Subsidized workers also show stronger labor-market attachment. These findings suggest demand-side interventions can complement supply-side policies in addressing gender gaps.

b3ea4f41ab:f5dbb2e01c19c7e0.title: Ideas and Firm Dynamics When It Takes Two to Tango
b3ea4f41ab:f5dbb2e01c19c7e0.author: Honghao Wang
b3ea4f41ab:f5dbb2e01c19c7e0.summary: Teams of inventors now produce over 80 percent of U.S. patents, up from just 45 percent in 1976. Over the same period, inventor employment has become increasingly concentrated in large firms, rising six times more than overall employment concentration. To explain these trends, we develop a new model of endogenous team formation within firms and embed it in a general equilibrium model of the inventor labor market. Teams increase firms’ returns to scale by increasing the likelihood of productive matches between inventors. The value of these matches rises over time, possibly driven by increasing knowledge specialization. This causes large firms to expand and small firms to shrink in equilibrium, accounting for the observed increase in inventor employment concentration. Because firms do not internalize knowledge spillovers, there is misallocation of inventors across firms. The rise of team production amplifies this misallocation by a factor of six by reallocating inventors away from small firms that generate disproportionately large knowledge spillovers.

b3ea4f41ab:6d32517dc3ca1324.title: Daily Team Behaviors as Predictors of Team Effectiveness Outcomes: Evidence from a Technology Entrepreneurship Incubator Program
b3ea4f41ab:6d32517dc3ca1324.author: Sommerville, Gillian
b3ea4f41ab:6d32517dc3ca1324.summary: Team effectiveness in high-stakes, time-limited work contexts remains an underexplored area of organizational and applied psychology research. This study examined whether daily process behaviors—specifically team communication and collaboration—predict end-of-program team effectiveness outcomes in the context of an intensive, eight-week technology entrepreneurship incubator program. Participants were members of five start-up teams enrolled in the start-up program at a large research university. As part of a larger mixed-methods study, participants completed daily diary measures of team communication and collaboration using a digital platform (Metricwire) for 15 days. At program end, participants completed a post-program survey assessing team effectiveness outcomes including creativity, psychological safety, team viability, collective efficacy, authentic relationships, opportunities for growth, and program satisfaction. Simple linear regressions revealed that daily collaboration significantly predicted creativity, psychological safety, team viability, and collective efficacy. Daily communication similarly predicted creativity and psychological safety. Authentic relationships were not significantly predicted by either behavioral measure. These findings contribute to the growing literature on team process and performance by demonstrating that observable daily team behaviors capture meaningful variance in team effectiveness outcomes, Implications for team-based intervention design and digital measurement methodology are discussed.

b3ea4f41ab:9dc5a2ab510ffd27.title: Staged financing beyond the venture record: Equity rounds in the accounts of Italian SMEs
b3ea4f41ab:9dc5a2ab510ffd27.author: Plantamura, Antonio Volpe
b3ea4f41ab:9dc5a2ab510ffd27.summary: Almost everything known about equity rounds in young firms comes from the records of professional investors, so the evidence is selected on the presence of an intermediary. We read rounds instead from the share-premium reserve, a compulsory, disclosed and restricted line of the Italian statutory balance sheet, for 3, 225 certified innovative SMEs over 2016–2025: 2, 991 priced capital increases on 1, 330 firms. Firms about to raise grew twice as fast in the preceding year and held identical cash, yet six in ten closed it at a loss; profitability falls and intangible assets rise only after the round. Seven panel estimators place the association across firms and not within them; a taxonomy estimated blind to the event finds the mechanism in all five financial configurations, with incidence differing eightfold; six flexible learners fail to improve on the linear specification. Selection operates on growth, not on profitability, a distinction intermediated samples cannot see.

b3ea4f41ab:e45ca219d21a6c19.author: Michael S. Barr

b3ea4f41ab:ccc1b43bbb0574e0.title: Female Micro-Entrepreneurship and Child Development
b3ea4f41ab:ccc1b43bbb0574e0.author: Hyun Soo Suh
b3ea4f41ab:ccc1b43bbb0574e0.summary: Ultra-poor graduation programs (UPG) reliably reduce extreme poverty among adult recipients, yet their intergenerational effects on children remain largely undocumented. We study a child-focused UPG in rural Malawi that augments the standard graduation bundle with early childhood development (ECD) training, targeting mothers with young children in a population that is both severely stunted and approximately 1 SD behind international benchmarks on cognitive and non-cognitive development. In an RCT of 1, 872 households, we show that the intervention raises child development by 0.16 to 0.26 SD within one year but has no significant effects on anthropometrics. Behind the impacts is a broad shift in parental inputs and behaviors. The results demonstrate that a child-focused anti-poverty program can generate child development gains that have not been documented in comparable programs without a child focus.

b3ea4f41ab:0233e7d7c0ef6313.title: Innovation in the financial industry: fintech and venture capital
b3ea4f41ab:0233e7d7c0ef6313.author: Diego Scalise
b3ea4f41ab:0233e7d7c0ef6313.summary: Technological innovation has profoundly transformed financial services. This paper examines the diffusion of technology-intensive firms operating in the financial sector (fintech) and the pivotal role of venture capital in supporting their development. The analysis reveals an ecosystem predominantly consisting of small fintech firms, which cluster in the financial centres of countries with more developed capital markets. These locations are home, in particular, to business-to-business (B2B) firms, which frequently develop digital solutions for financial institutions. In this environment, incumbent financial intermediaries become the natural acquirers of the most promising fintech start-ups, integrating their technologies and capabilities into their value chains. Access to diversified sources of finance is a key determinant of these firms' growth. Venture capital acts as a catalyst by fostering strategic partnerships and facilitating the integration of innovative technologies, thereby contributing to the transformation of traditional financial intermediation. The distribution of fintech firms and the evolution of their financing cycle portray a sector undergoing a transition from an initial phase of rapid expansion to one of gradual consolidation.

b3ea4f41ab:eddf5bff75f093f0.title: Innovate to Borrow: How Intangibles Shape Finance and Growth
b3ea4f41ab:eddf5bff75f093f0.author: Victoria Vanasco
b3ea4f41ab:eddf5bff75f093f0.summary: We study a dynamic economy in which heterogeneous entrepreneurs invest in either generic or innovative technologies, the latter relying on intangible, firm-specific assets whose payoffs are realized through learning or experimentation (e.g., know-how, R&D). A key friction is that, to finance investment, entrepreneurs can pledge assets but not cash flows. We show that innovative technologies can relax financing constraints by increasing the value of continuation relative to default, thereby enabling borrowing against future cash flows. Technology choice is non-monotonic in productivity: low-productivity entrepreneurs innovate-to-experiment and delay investment, intermediate types adopt generic technologies, and high-productivity entrepreneurs innovate-to-scale and relax financial constraints. In equilibrium, financial frictions distort both the allocation of capital and the choice of technology, leading to insuﬀicient experimentation. The model helps us understand how innovation is adopted across firms and economies and has novel policy implications.

b3ea4f41ab:0d7f012743a21b1c.title: What Does Venture Capital Actually Finance ? Scale and Structure around the World
b3ea4f41ab:0d7f012743a21b1c.author: Mauro, Paolo
b3ea4f41ab:0d7f012743a21b1c.summary: Venture capital is widely viewed as financing knowledge-intensive, R&D-driven startups, but owing to data constraints, this view has been based largely on high-income economies. By taking a global perspective, this paper documents that what venture capital finances differs systematically across economies, varying with institutional and business conditions rather than following a single model. Using a new cross-country dataset that harmonizes firm-level venture capital records with equity issuance data for more than 150 economies, the data shows that VC markets differ across countries not only in scale but in kind. Outside high-income countries, rather than being concentrated in knowledge intangibles, venture capital tilts–at both the sector and firm levels–toward organizational intangibles such as distribution, logistics, and payments. Highlighting the unique features of venture capital, this pattern is absent from public equity markets, where sectoral composition is far more similar across income levels. An accounting decomposition separates venture capital depth into the rate at which firms enter the market and the funding each entrant attracts, and entry accounts for the largest cross-country gaps. Moreover, the business environment is associated with VC primarily through entry, linked both to the size of the market and to the composition of what venture capital finances, the latter through entry into knowledge-intensive sectors in particular.

b3ea4f41ab:2a06d7f88084c3e1.title: How do firms cope with economic shocks in real time?
b3ea4f41ab:2a06d7f88084c3e1.author: Ivan Yotzov
b3ea4f41ab:2a06d7f88084c3e1.summary: In a turbulent world, effective policy requires granular estimates of firm responses to shocks as they unfold. We develop a replicable framework that combines high-frequency administrative and survey microdata with a pre-registered shift-share design to estimate multi-margin firm responses in real time. We show that the resulting coefficient vectors can be interpreted as first-order perturbations of firms’ optimal-response functions. We apply the framework to the 2021–23 UK energy price shock and find that energy-intensive firms pass on cost increases, build cash reserves and shift towards homeworking. We find little evidence of aggregate employment losses or firm exits. Responses are highly heterogeneous: small firms drive price pass-through; large firms, capital investment. We show that our real-time estimates are consistent with the UK’s structural business survey, released two years later, and across survey instruments. We apply the framework out of sample and in real time to the energy price shock triggered by the 2026 US–Israeli strikes on Iran and discuss implications for the design of energy support schemes and environmental policy.

b3ea4f41ab:a721cbf57afaacef.title: Revisiting the Risk-Return Relationship in Venture Capital: Market Cycles, Investor Heterogeneity and Regional Environments
b3ea4f41ab:a721cbf57afaacef.author: Hennings, Christian Hermann
b3ea4f41ab:a721cbf57afaacef.summary: Venture capital (VC) plays a central role in financing entrepreneurial ventures. Despite its importance, the relationship between risk and return remains difficult to explain by standard financial theory. Standard asset pricing theory conceptualizes risk as an ex-ante, observable characteristic that is compensated by expected returns through a stable, separable relationship. However, in VC markets illiquidity, staged financing, information asymmetries, and highly skewed payoff distributions violate these assumptions. Risk and return are jointly determined by financing dynamics, investor heterogeneity, and market conditions, so that realized returns reflect a combination of technological, financing, timing, and macroeconomic risks. This dissertation advances the argument that the risk-return relationship in VC is not a stable trade-off but varies systematically with financing conditions and investor composition. The seven empirical chapters collectively examine how staged financing, capital supply dynamics, and regional and organizational heterogeneity across investor types influence observed performance patterns. The findings show that risk and return in VC are shaped by market conditions, investor structure, and regional environments. Expansionary periods increase venture survival and delay the realization of downside risk. In contrast, contractionary periods reduce capital supply and accelerate selection. Consequently, identical underlying venture risk may result in different observed performance outcomes, depending on the prevailing market regime, the type of investor providing capital, and the institutional and financial depth of the regional ecosystem. Differences in investor resources, organizational form, and regional institutional frameworks systematically affect funding continuity, exit timing, and the distribution of realized returns. Overall, this dissertation contributes a unified framework that integrates insights from asset pricing, entrepreneurial…
